questions.stem: The ANZUS Treaty, signed in 1951, was an alliance between:
options: Australia, New Zealand and the United States
Australia, New Zealand and the United Kingdom
Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States
Australia, New Zealand and the nations of South-East Asia
questions.explanation: ANZUS linked Australia, New Zealand and the United States. Britain was not a member, which marked Australia's shift towards the United States as its main ally.

questions.stem: Under ANZUS, what did each member promise if another was attacked in the Pacific?
options: To place its armed forces under a single joint command based in Washington
To station troops permanently on the territory of each of the other two members
To act to meet the common danger in accordance with its constitutional processes
To declare war automatically on any state that attacked another member in the Pacific
questions.explanation: ANZUS committed members to consult and to act according to their own constitutional processes, which is weaker than an automatic promise to go to war. Debate over how much protection it really guaranteed has continued ever since.

questions.stem: Australia signed ANZUS in the same year as the peace treaty with Japan. Which interpretation of Australia's motives is best supported by this context?
options: Australia joined ANZUS because the United Nations required Pacific nations to form regional pacts
Australia wanted the treaty mainly to gain US funding for its post-war immigration programs
Australia wanted a US security guarantee as reassurance against a possible revived Japan and against communism
Australia wanted ANZUS so that it could leave the Commonwealth and end all its remaining defence ties with Britain
questions.explanation: Many Australians feared a lenient peace with Japan, and the government also feared communism in Asia. A guarantee from the United States addressed both. Australia kept its Commonwealth links and its defence ties with Britain, for example in Malaya.

questions.stem: The Southeast Asia Treaty Organization (SEATO), formed in 1954, aimed mainly to:
options: settle border disputes between India and Pakistan
contain the spread of communism in South-East Asia
promote free trade among the nations of South-East Asia
end European colonial rule in South-East Asia
questions.explanation: SEATO, created by the Manila Pact, was a Cold War alliance to resist communist expansion in the region. Its members included Australia, New Zealand, the United States, Britain and France, and a protocol extended its protection to South Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia.

questions.stem: Australian forces fought in Korea from 1950 to 1953. Under whose authority were they committed?
options: The SEATO alliance, which required all of its members to defend South Korea against communist attack
A British Commonwealth request to protect British colonies in East Asia from China
The ANZUS Treaty, which obliged Australia to support any US military action in Asia
A United Nations command, led by the United States, resisting North Korea's invasion of the South
questions.explanation: When North Korea invaded the South in June 1950, the UN Security Council called on members to help, and Australia joined the US-led UN command. SEATO did not yet exist, and ANZUS was signed after the war began.

questions.stem: During the Malayan Emergency, Australian air and ground forces fought alongside British and New Zealand forces against:
options: communist insurgents fighting to take control of Malaya
Indonesian forces attempting to occupy the island of Borneo
Japanese forces that had refused to surrender after 1945
North Vietnamese forces moving south through Malaya
questions.explanation: The Emergency (1948–60) was a guerrilla war against the Malayan communists. Australian army battalions served from 1955 in the Far East Strategic Reserve. Fighting Indonesia in Borneo was Confrontation, in the 1960s.

questions.stem: In April 1965 the Menzies government announced that it would send:
options: a naval task force to blockade the coast of North Vietnam
conscripted soldiers to serve under the SEATO flag in Laos
an infantry battalion to fight in South Vietnam
the first military advisers to train South Vietnamese troops
questions.explanation: Menzies announced on 29 April 1965 that 1RAR would be sent to Vietnam. Australian military advisers had been there since 1962, so the battalion marked an escalation from advising to combat.

questions.stem: The National Service Act 1964 required 20-year-old men to register, then selected them for service by:
options: a ballot drawn by date of birth
a written test of physical fitness
the order in which they registered
a choice made by their employers
questions.explanation: Marbles representing birth dates were drawn in a ballot, and men whose birthdays came up were called up for two years' service. Critics called it a 'lottery of death', since conscripts could be sent to Vietnam.

questions.stem: What change in 1965 made the 1964 National Service scheme very different from the scheme of the 1950s?
options: Conscripts could now be sent to serve overseas, including in Vietnam
Women were now required to register for National Service as well as men
Conscripts could now choose to serve in the navy rather than the army
The ballot was replaced by compulsory service for all young men
questions.explanation: An amendment to the Defence Act in 1965 allowed national servicemen to be sent overseas. The 1951 scheme had been home-based training, so the change revived the old Australian debate about conscription for service abroad.

questions.stem: How did the Whitlam government change National Service soon after taking office in December 1972?
options: It abolished conscription and released men jailed for refusing to serve
It extended conscription to women and sent them to serve in non-combat roles
It replaced the birth date ballot with compulsory service for all
It kept conscription but stopped conscripts serving overseas
questions.explanation: Whitlam's government ended conscription, freed draft resisters and withdrew the remaining Australian military advisers from Vietnam. Labor had campaigned against conscription and the war since 1965.

questions.stem: The Welcome Home parade held in Sydney on 3 October 1987 honoured:
options: World War Two prisoners of war on the anniversary of their release
Vietnam veterans, many of whom felt they had been ignored on their return
Korean War veterans returning from the armistice line after 1953
Australian peacekeepers returning from the United Nations mission in Cambodia
questions.explanation: Many Vietnam veterans had come home to indifference or hostility. The 1987 parade was a public recognition of their service, followed in 1992 by the dedication of the national Vietnam memorial in Canberra.

questions.stem: The domino theory held that:
options: if one country in South-East Asia fell to communism, its neighbours would follow
communist movements in Asia would collapse once their leaders had been removed from power
Western nations should leave Asian countries to settle their own conflicts
Britain should remain the main power responsible for South-East Asia
questions.explanation: The theory, stated by US President Eisenhower in 1954, imagined countries falling one after another like dominoes. It was used to argue that Vietnam had to be defended to protect South-East Asia and ultimately Australia.

questions.stem: 'Forward defence' in Australian strategy during the 1950s and 1960s meant:
options: relying on the United Nations rather than alliances for security
fighting threats in South-East Asia before they could reach Australia
building up coastal forces to repel an invasion of northern Australia
staying neutral in Cold War conflicts to avoid making enemies in Asia
questions.explanation: Forward defence placed Australian forces in Malaya, Borneo and Vietnam, alongside 'great and powerful friends'. It was later replaced by a stress on the defence of Australia and self-reliance.

questions.stem: In 1951 the Menzies government held a referendum seeking power to ban the Communist Party. What does this event show about Australia in the early Cold War?
options: Fear of communism was so strong that voters approved the ban on the party by an overwhelming majority
The Communist Party was banned by the High Court, so the referendum merely confirmed it
The Labor Party supported the ban, and only the Communist Party campaigned against it
Fear of communism was strong, but voters narrowly refused to give the government that power
questions.explanation: After the High Court struck down the Communist Party Dissolution Act, the referendum to give the Commonwealth the power was narrowly defeated. Labor leader H. V. Evatt led the No case, arguing for civil liberties.

questions.stem: In 1969 US President Nixon said America's Asian allies should provide more of their own ground forces for their defence. How did this affect Australian defence thinking over the following two decades?
options: It caused Australia to send more conscripts to Vietnam to replace US troops
It led Australia to return to relying on Britain and its navy for its main protection in Asia
It pushed Australia from forward defence towards self-reliance and defence of the continent
It led Australia to withdraw from ANZUS and seek a neutral foreign policy
questions.explanation: The Guam Doctrine signalled the US would not fight every Asian ground war, so Australia increasingly planned for self-reliance, a shift reflected in the 1986 Dibb Review and 1987 Defence White Paper. Australia stayed in ANZUS, and Britain had already withdrawn east of Suez.

questions.stem: Which statement about the shift in Australia's alliances after 1945 is most accurate?
options: Australia ended all defence ties with Britain when it signed the ANZUS Treaty in 1951
Australia relied mainly on Britain for its defence until 1975, when it joined ANZUS for the first time
Australia avoided all formal alliances and relied only on the United Nations
Australia's main alliance moved from Britain to the United States, though ties with Britain continued
questions.explanation: The fall of Singapore and the Pacific War turned Australia towards the US, formalised in ANZUS. Australia still served with Britain in Korea, Malaya and Borneo, so the change was gradual rather than a clean break.

questions.stem: In 1949 the rule excluding people 'not substantially of European origin or descent' from the armed forces was removed. Which later development best reflects the same idea of equality for service personnel?
options: The withdrawal of Australian combat battalions from Vietnam in 1971
The signing of the SEATO treaty with Britain and the United States in 1954
The lifting of the ban on gay and lesbian people serving in the defence force in 1992
The introduction of a birth date ballot to select which young men would do National Service from 1964
questions.explanation: Both changes removed a barrier to who could serve in the armed forces. The ballot and the withdrawal from Vietnam were about how many served and where, not equal treatment of service personnel.

questions.stem: The National Service scheme introduced in 1951 required 18-year-old men to:
options: enlist in the regular army for six years and serve wherever they were sent
undergo military training in Australia, without being sent overseas
serve two years with the army in Korea or Malaya
join the Communist Party Dissolution taskforce
questions.explanation: The 1951 scheme gave young men a period of training for home defence and did not send them overseas. It ended in 1959, and conscription for overseas service only returned with the 1964 Act and the 1965 amendment.

questions.stem: In 1965 Labor leader Arthur Calwell told parliament that Labor did not think the commitment of troops to Vietnam was wise, timely or right. Which argument did he also make?
options: That Australia should leave SEATO and ANZUS once the war was over
That the commitment would not help the fight against communism
That Australia should send conscripts to Vietnam instead of regular soldiers
That Britain, not Australia, should take responsibility for defending Malaya
questions.explanation: Calwell argued the decision was wrong and would not help the fight against communism. He was also a long-time opponent of conscription, and Labor opposed sending conscripts to Vietnam.

questions.stem: In the 1966 federal election Harold Holt's government, which strongly supported the Vietnam commitment, won a large victory over Calwell's Labor. A historian could best use this result as evidence that:
options: Labor had changed its policy to support sending conscripts to Vietnam before the election
in 1966 most voters accepted the government's case for the war and National Service
opposition to the war had become the majority view among Australian voters by 1966
the Moratorium marches had forced the government to promise withdrawal from Vietnam
questions.explanation: The 1966 result suggests broad support for the war at that time. Opposition grew later in the decade, peaking with the Moratorium marches of 1970–71, which came after this election.

questions.stem: The Democratic Labor Party (DLP), formed after the Labor split of 1955, took which position on the Vietnam War?
options: Strong support, based on its anti-communism
Strong opposition, based on its pacifism
Support for Britain fighting, but not Australia
Neutrality, leaving the decision to the UN
questions.explanation: The DLP, with strong roots in Catholic anti-communism, backed the war and conscription. Its preferences helped keep the Coalition in government through the 1960s.

questions.stem: Australia's commitments to the United Nations after 1950 included:
options: a permanent seat on the UN Security Council from 1950
providing the main ground forces for the UN in Vietnam
a formal promise never to fight a war without first gaining a UN resolution
peacekeeping missions, such as in Kashmir and later in Cambodia
questions.explanation: Australia sent observers to Kashmir from 1950 and played a leading part in the UN mission in Cambodia in the early 1990s. The Vietnam War was not a UN operation, which some critics pointed to when opposing it.

questions.stem: Critics of Australia's role in the 1990–91 Gulf War accepted that it had United Nations approval, but still raised concerns. Which concern most closely echoed earlier debates about Vietnam?
options: That conscripts would be sent to fight in the Middle East under a newly introduced ballot system
That the war would bring a Japanese invasion of northern Australia
That Australia was joining a US-led war mainly to keep its alliance with the United States
That Australia had no legal power to send naval ships without a referendum of all voters
questions.explanation: Some critics argued Australia followed the United States into the Gulf as it had into Vietnam, to keep the alliance. The Gulf commitment used regular forces, not conscripts, and no referendum was needed.

questions.stem: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander men who served in Korea and Vietnam often described equality in the ranks. Which statement best describes many of them on returning home?
options: They still faced discrimination and restrictions in civilian life
They were all granted land under a special soldier settlement scheme
They were automatically exempted from state protection laws by the RSL
They were awarded full veterans' pensions before any other servicemen
questions.explanation: Many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander servicemen found that the respect they had earned in uniform did not protect them from discrimination at home. Their experiences fed into wider campaigns for civil rights.

questions.stem: During the Vietnam War, women in the Australian armed forces served mainly as:
options: fighter pilots flying missions over North Vietnam
nurses and in support roles, not in combat units
combat soldiers in infantry battalions at Nui Dat
conscripts selected by the same ballot as men
questions.explanation: Army and RAAF nurses served in Vietnam, and women's services provided support roles. Women were excluded from combat, and only men were subject to National Service.

questions.stem: In November 1992 the Keating government ended the ban on which group serving in the Australian Defence Force?
options: People born overseas
Gay and lesbian people
Married women
Aboriginal people
questions.explanation: Lifting the ban let gay and lesbian personnel serve openly. Racial restrictions on enlistment had been lifted in 1949, and married women were already able to serve by 1992.

questions.stem: From the early 1950s many servicewomen belonged to separate women's services, such as the WRAAC and the WRANS. What happened to these two services in the 1980s?
options: They were merged into a single civilian auxiliary run by the Red Cross
They were disbanded and their members were integrated into the regular army and navy
They were expanded into combat units that served alongside men in Vietnam
They were abolished and women were again banned from every form of military service
questions.explanation: In the 1980s the separate women's services were absorbed into the regular forces, so women served in the same structure as men. Combat roles remained closed to women for years after.

questions.stem: A historian claims that 'Vietnam was Australia's first television war'. Which evidence would best support the claim that the media influenced Australian opinion on Vietnam?
options: The government owned all TV stations and used them to recruit volunteers
TV footage of events such as the Tet Offensive raised doubts about official claims of progress
Strict censorship stopped any footage of fighting being shown in Australian homes
Newspapers refused to report on the fighting until all Australian troops had been withdrawn from Vietnam
questions.explanation: Television brought the war into homes, and footage of events like the 1968 Tet Offensive contrasted with official claims that the war was being won. Censorship was far looser than in the world wars, and commercial stations were privately owned.

questions.stem: Conscientious objectors under the National Service Act could gain exemption only if they:
options: had a parent who had served in World War Two
objected to all wars, not just the war in Vietnam
had already served in the citizen military forces
were enrolled at a university or teachers' college
questions.explanation: The Act recognised only objection to all war, so men who opposed Vietnam in particular had no legal way out. Students could defer service, but deferral was not exemption.

questions.stem: Save Our Sons, formed in Sydney in 1965, was a movement of mainly:
options: church leaders supporting the war against communism
women, many of them mothers, opposing conscription for Vietnam
young men refusing to register for National Service
Vietnam veterans demanding better repatriation benefits
questions.explanation: Save Our Sons drew on mothers' concern for their sons, using vigils, leaflets and petitions. Its respectable image made opposition to conscription harder to dismiss as radical.

questions.stem: In 1971 five Save Our Sons members, known as the Fairlea Five, were jailed. What had they done?
options: Stood as candidates against the government in the 1969 federal election
Handed out anti-conscription leaflets at a Commonwealth office in Melbourne
Organised the first Moratorium march down Melbourne's Bourke Street in May 1970
Sheltered young men who had been called up and gone into hiding
questions.explanation: The women were jailed in Fairlea prison for distributing leaflets urging young men not to register. Their imprisonment drew wide publicity and sympathy for the anti-conscription cause.

questions.stem: The Vietnam Moratorium marches of 1970 and 1971 were known mainly for:
options: mass peaceful street protests calling for the war to end
violent attacks on army barracks in capital cities
secret campaigns run only by university students
rallies supporting the government's war policy
questions.explanation: The first Moratorium on 8 May 1970 brought very large crowds into the streets of Melbourne and other cities, led in Melbourne by Labor's Jim Cairns. The marches drew on a broad coalition, not only students.

questions.stem: Before the first Moratorium, government ministers warned that the protests would lead to violence and disorder. The march in Melbourne passed largely peacefully. How might a historian use this contrast?
options: As evidence that the Moratorium was organised by the government itself
As proof that most Australians supported the war in 1970
As evidence that the protest movement had broad and respectable support
As proof that the government had changed its policy before the march
questions.explanation: A large, mainly peaceful march undermined claims that protesters were a violent fringe and showed how far opposition had spread. The government did not change its policy before the march, though withdrawals were already under way.

questions.stem: Many Vietnam veterans felt they were treated differently from veterans of the world wars when they returned. Which experience is most often reported?
options: Automatic grants of farmland under a soldier settlement scheme
Exemption from income tax for the rest of their working lives
Indifference or hostility from parts of the community and some RSL clubs
Large public victory parades in every capital city as each unit came home
questions.explanation: Veterans returned in small groups, often to a divided public, and some felt unwelcome in RSL clubs. That sense of neglect lay behind the 1987 Welcome Home parade.

questions.stem: In the late 1970s and 1980s Vietnam veterans' groups campaigned about health problems they linked to the war, especially:
options: exposure to chemical defoliants such as Agent Orange
malnutrition suffered in Japanese prisoner-of-war camps
radiation from British atomic tests in central Australia
influenza contracted while returning by troopship
questions.explanation: Veterans argued that defoliants used in Vietnam had harmed their health and their children's. A royal commission examined the issue in the 1980s, and the dispute shaped later recognition of veterans' health.

questions.stem: Alan Seymour's play 'The One Day of the Year' (first staged in 1960) and Redgum's song 'I Was Only Nineteen' (1983) both reflect which change in Australian culture?
options: A belief that Australia should rely on conscription for defence
Growing support for sending troops to fight in South-East Asia
A willingness to question war and its costs, not only to celebrate it
A return to the imperial loyalty that marked Australia in 1914
questions.explanation: Seymour's play questioned Anzac Day through a family conflict, and Redgum's song told of a young soldier's experience in Vietnam and its lasting effects. Both show popular culture examining war's human cost.

questions.stem: Attendance at Anzac Day marches fell in the 1960s and 1970s but grew again from the 1980s. Which factor helps explain the revival?
options: A new federal law making attendance at Anzac Day marches compulsory for all school students
The return of conscription for overseas service in the 1980s
A decision to hold Anzac Day only at the Australian War Memorial
Wider inclusion, such as Vietnam veterans' recognition and families marching
questions.explanation: Recognition of Vietnam veterans after 1987, interest from younger generations and descendants, and government support for commemoration all helped revive Anzac Day. There was no compulsion and no return of conscription.

questions.stem: What was dedicated in Canberra on 3 October 1992?
options: The Australian Vietnam Forces National Memorial
The Tomb of the Unknown Australian Soldier
The Korean War National Memorial
The Australian War Memorial building
questions.explanation: The Vietnam memorial on Anzac Parade was dedicated five years to the day after the Welcome Home parade. The Australian War Memorial had opened in 1941, and the Unknown Soldier was entombed in 1993.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates continuity in Australian debates about conscription between 1916 and 1972?
options: Australians consistently supported conscription for overseas service in every conflict
Debate about conscription ended in 1943 when militia were allowed to serve abroad
Conscription was always opposed only by the Catholic Church and no other groups
Compulsion to serve overseas remained deeply divisive, from the referendums to Vietnam
questions.explanation: The defeated referendums of 1916–17, the Labor dispute over the 1943 Act and the protests against the 1964 scheme all turned on sending conscripts abroad. Opponents came from many groups, including unions, women's movements and churches.

questions.stem: Which comparison best shows change in Australia's reasons for going to war between 1914 and the 1960s?
options: Fear of Germany gave way to fear of Britain and France as the main threats to Australian security
Support for the United Nations gave way to loyalty to the British Empire
Defence of Australia's own coastline gave way to neutrality in all foreign wars
Duty to the British Empire gave way to US alliance obligations and fear of communism in Asia
questions.explanation: In 1914 Australia went to war automatically as part of the Empire. By the 1960s, Australia's commitments to Vietnam were shaped by ANZUS, SEATO, forward defence and the domino theory.

questions.stem: A student argues that 'women's roles in war changed completely between 1914 and 1992'. Which evidence most weakens this claim?
options: Women formed their own armed services during World War Two
Women were integrated into the regular armed forces by the mid-1980s
Women were admitted to the armed forces on a permanent basis from the early 1950s
Women were still kept out of combat roles in 1992, as they had been in both world wars
questions.explanation: Women's military roles grew from nursing to auxiliary services to integration in the regular forces, but combat roles stayed closed through 1992, which shows continuity. The other developments are evidence of change rather than continuity.
